tool.name: CenterlineAndWidth

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/geometric-tools/centerline-and-width.html
Collapses polygons -- rivers, canals, corridors, valley bottoms -- to their centerlines, carrying the local polygon width along every result. Outputs either the main centerline (the longest path through the polygon's medial axis) or the full branched skeleton with tributary branches, short boundary-noise spurs pruned. Every line carries minimum / mean / maximum width in meters; optional station points carry the exact width at evenly spaced stations (the width profile), and optional segments carry width statistics per piece for graduated-color width maps. Holes are handled natively -- the skeleton simply routes around islands -- any attribute fields transfer from the source polygons, and line ends can extend to the polygon boundary. A license-free replacement for Esri's Polygon To Centerline. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
Collapses each polygon to the line down its middle -- and, because the construction knows the distance to the boundary at every step, every output carries the polygon's width as well. Rivers and canals become centerlines with a width profile; wildlife corridors, canyon bottoms and habitat strips become measurable transects.
How it works. The polygon boundary is sampled densely and its Voronoi diagram built; the Voronoi vertices and edges that lie inside the polygon are the polygon's medial axis -- the skeleton of points equidistant from two or more boundary edges -- and every skeleton vertex knows its clearance (half the local width). This is the same construction as the suite's Bottleneck Analysis tool; here, instead of the widest route between two blocks, the tool extracts: • The main centerline: the longest path through the skeleton (its length-weighted diameter) -- the natural source-to-mouth line of a river polygon. Where channels split and rejoin around an island, the route between the two ends follows the wider channel (each step is weighted by its length divided by the local width, the same rule as Bottleneck Analysis), not blindly the shorter one. • The full branched skeleton: every branch, split into separate line features at junctions, with each feature flagged (IsTrunk) whether it lies on the main centerline -- so tributaries are kept but the main stem is one selection away. Side spurs shorter than the minimum branch length are pruned (blank = automatic, tuned to remove boundary-noise whiskers only).
Widths everywhere. Each line carries MinW_m / MeanW_m / MaxW_m plus its geodesic Length_m, all in meters. The optional station points output places evenly spaced stations along every line (the spacing is yours; blank = the main centerline's length / 100, shared by its branches so station density stays uniform), each with its distance along the line (Station_m) and the exact polygon width there (Width_m) -- the full width profile, ready for charts or joins. The optional segments output dices the centerline at those same stations, each piece carrying its own width statistics -- symbolize it with graduated colors and the river paints its own narrows.
Attribute transfer. Pick any of the source polygon's fields and every output feature carries them, alongside an automatic Src_FID (the source polygon's Object ID) and a Line_ID shared by the line, its station points and its segments. Fields whose names are reserved on the output (OBJECTID, Shape_Length, Shape_Area...) or that collide with the tool's own fields still transfer -- their source values arrive under a Src_ prefix (Src_Shape_Area holds the source polygon's area, not anything about the line), truncated and uniquified for shapefiles' 10-character field names. Geometry fields cannot transfer as attributes and are reported.
Ends, smoothing, detail. A medial axis stops short of a polygon's end caps; with Extend the line ends on (the default), each free tip is carried out to the boundary, so river centerlines reach their mouths (the near-zero widths on those short extension stubs are excluded from the line's width statistics). Light smoothing relaxes the raw skeleton's jaggedness without ever letting the line leave the polygon (blank = automatic; 0 = off). The Advanced Detail distance is the boundary sampling spacing: smaller values resolve finer necks and tighter bends at more computing cost; if a warning reports the skeleton splitting into pieces at thin pinch points, lower it.
Holes and shapes. Interior holes need no preprocessing: the skeleton routes around islands, and a ring skeleton circling a hole is written as a closed line. Multipart polygons yield one centerline per part (the Part field tells them apart); every polygon in the input is processed (layer selections honored). True-curve boundaries are densified automatically. Geographic (latitude/longitude) inputs are processed in a feature-centered equidistant projection, so all widths and lengths are honest meters.
Relation to Esri's tool. Esri's Polygon To Centerline (Topographic Production toolbox) requires Standard or Advanced plus the Production Mapping extension; this tool runs at every license level. Esri's tool transfers no attributes beyond an FID link -- here any fields transfer, and every output carries width, which Esri's tool does not compute at all. Esri's documentation directs users to remove interior holes with Eliminate Polygon Part before running (destroying real islands); this tool handles holes natively. Esri's tool supports neither shapefile output nor true-curve input; this tool supports both. Esri's Connecting Features parameter (snapping centerlines into an existing hydro network with flow direction) is the one capability not replicated here.

dialogReference.para: The polygons to collapse to centerlines -- rivers, canals, corridors, valley bottoms. Every polygon is processed; a layer selection is honored. Holes are fine (the skeleton routes around islands).
Main centerline only: the longest path through the polygon's skeleton -- the source-to-mouth line.
Full branched skeleton: every branch as its own feature, split at junctions, short spurs pruned; the IsTrunk field flags the main line's pieces.

param.name: transfer_fields
param.displayname: Attribute fields to transfer to every output

dialogReference.para: Any of the source polygon's fields; their values are copied onto every centerline, station point and segment, alongside the automatic Src_FID.

Reserved or conflicting names (Shape_Length, Shape_Area, or a field matching one of the tool's own) transfer under a Src_ prefix with the source values intact -- e.g. Src_Shape_Area is the source polygon's area. Names are truncated for shapefiles. The ObjectID field is not offered here because Src_FID already carries it (a scripted call may still pass OBJECTID and receives Src_OBJECTID).

param.name: min_branch
param.displayname: Minimum branch length (skeleton mode: shorter side spurs are pruned; blank = automatic)

dialogReference.para: Skeleton mode: side branches shorter than this are pruned as boundary noise. Blank = automatic (removes only sampling-scale whiskers); larger values keep only substantial tributaries. Branches on the main centerline are never pruned.

Choosing a value -- picture a river polygon about 100 m wide. Every irregularity in the bank (a cove, a backwater pocket, a stub of a side channel) sprouts its own short skeleton branch, roughly as long as the feature it reaches into. Left blank, only the tiny jaggedness whiskers vanish, so all of those coves keep their branches -- the fullest skeleton. At 100 m (about the river's width), branches into mere bank features disappear and what survives are genuine side channels and tributary arms longer than the river is wide -- usually the natural choice. At 1,000 m, only major arms at least a kilometer long remain, collapsing a braided or ragged reach to its main stem and principal branches. In short: set it to the smallest side feature you would want to see as its own line, in the units chosen below.

param.name: extend_ends
param.displayname: Extend the line ends to the polygon boundary

dialogReference.para: A medial axis stops short of the polygon's end caps; this carries each free line tip out to the boundary, so river centerlines reach their mouths. The near-zero widths on the short extension stubs are excluded from the line's width statistics.

param.name: smoothing
param.displayname: Smoothing distance (blank = automatic light smoothing; 0 = none)

dialogReference.para: Relaxes the raw skeleton's jaggedness with a moving average over this distance -- without ever letting the line leave the polygon. Blank = automatic light smoothing; 0 = the raw skeleton.

param.name: station_spacing
param.displayname: Station spacing for the point and segment outputs (blank = 100 stations along the main centerline; branches share that spacing)

dialogReference.para: The distance between width stations along each line, for the station-point and segment outputs. Blank = the main centerline's length divided by 100, applied as the same spacing to every branch (computed per polygon) -- so the trunk gets about 100 stations, a branch half its length gets about 50, and a short spur gets its two endpoints, keeping station density uniform across the whole skeleton instead of piling 100 stations onto every little branch.
Units for the minimum branch length, smoothing distance, station spacing and Detail: Meters, Kilometers, Feet or Miles. Output width and length fields are always in meters.
The centerlines: Line_ID, Src_FID, Part, IsTrunk, geodesic Length_m, and MinW_m / MeanW_m / MaxW_m (meters), plus any transferred fields.
Evenly spaced stations along every centerline, each with Station_m (distance along the line) and Width_m (the exact polygon width there) -- the width profile.
The centerline diced at the stations, each piece with its own MinW_m / MeanW_m / MaxW_m -- ready for graduated-color width mapping.

param.name: boundary_step
param.displayname: Detail: boundary sampling distance (blank = automatic; smaller = finer centerline, slower)

dialogReference.para: Advanced: the boundary sampling spacing that controls the skeleton's fidelity (blank = automatic, about 1/2000 of each polygon's extent diagonal). Lower it when thin necks disconnect the skeleton or tight bends cut corners.

scriptExample.title: Centerline and Width example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: A river polygon collapsed to its main centerline with a width profile every 100 m, carrying the river's name.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # mode options (matching is by prefix): # "Main centerline only" # "Full branched skeleton (with tributary branches)" # linear_units: "Meters" / "Kilometers" / "Feet" / "Miles" # (applies to min_branch, smoothing, station_spacing, boundary_step; # output width/length FIELDS are always meters) arcpy.jenness.CenterlineAndWidth( in_features=r"D:\data\hydro.gdb\river_polys", mode="Main centerline only", transfer_fields="GNIS_Name", extend_ends=True, station_spacing=100.0, linear_units="Meters", out_lines=r"D:\data\hydro.gdb\river_centerlines", out_points=r"D:\data\hydro.gdb\river_width_stations", out_segments=r"D:\data\hydro.gdb\river_width_segments")
